hook.question_in_my_head: Why would a smith lay his shield in the dirt every day while an army is outside the city? What is he doing?
hook.why: The image is odd and concrete against the stakes of a siege; 'bronze-smith' and 'the city's' are slightly vague.

who.bronze_smith: A smith inside a besieged city who listens with his shield; his goal is only implied until the end: find the Persians' tunnel.
who.city_guards_defenders: Laugh at him; later 'the defenders' dig down into the tunnel.
who.persian_army: Besieging Barca; pound the walls in the open and secretly dig a tunnel under them.

what_happened: A Persian army besieges the city of Barca in ancient Libya, and the smith keeps putting his shield on the ground.
The guards think the siege has driven him mad.
For months the Persians pound the walls and fail, but they stay.
The smith walks along the inside of the wall, setting the shield down and listening at spot after spot.
A guard mocks him, saying the enemy is outside, not underground.
For days the shield only thuds.
At one spot the shield rings and the dust on it trembles.
We learn the Persians were secretly digging under the walls the whole time.
The defenders dig down wherever the shield rings and break into the tunnel from above.
The Persians' months of secret digging were detected by one shield.
why: A bronze shield on solid ground just thuds. Over a hollow tunnel with people swinging picks below, the shield picks up the vibrations and rings like a bell, so the ringing marks where an enemy tunnel is. The defenders dug down at those spots. I'm taking the physics on trust: the narration only asserts it.
twist: The enemy wasn't only attacking the walls from outside; they were secretly tunneling underneath, and the smith's 'crazy' shield behavior was how the city found out.
